title: CloudNest — Intelligent Edge Computing and Inference Optimization
content:
CloudNest is the inference optimization platform that makes AI faster and cheaper at the edge. We enable enterprises to run AI workloads where they perform best — dynamically routing inference between edge nodes and cloud infrastructure based on real-time latency, cost, and accuracy requirements.

As AI moves from experimentation to production, enterprises face a fundamental trade-off: cloud inference is flexible but expensive and slow; edge inference is fast but limited in capability. CloudNest eliminates this trade-off with an intelligent routing engine that automatically splits and distributes model inference across heterogeneous infrastructure.

Our platform reduces AI inference costs by up to 60% while improving latency for real-time applications. We achieve this through proprietary model-splitting algorithms that dynamically partition neural networks across edge and cloud nodes, optimizing for each workload's specific requirements.

Founded in 2023 by Natasha Volkov, former AWS edge computing product lead, and Kai Tanaka, formerly of NVIDIA's inference optimization team, CloudNest combines deep infrastructure expertise with ML systems innovation. Our team of 35 engineers across Berlin and San Francisco serves 18 enterprise customers, including Fortune 500 companies in automotive, manufacturing, and financial services.

CloudNest integrates seamlessly into existing ML pipelines through a lightweight SDK. No infrastructure changes required — just drop in and start saving.

title: CloudNest — First Meeting with Natasha Volkov (CEO)
author: Sarah Chen
content:
Meeting: Introduction — CloudNest
Date: February 20, 2026
Attendees: Sarah Chen (AIVC), Natasha Volkov (CEO, CloudNest)
Location: TechCrunch Berlin conference, side meeting

## Summary

Met Natasha at the TC Berlin event. She's one of the most technically sharp CEOs I've met this year — built the edge computing product at AWS that now serves thousands of enterprise customers. Left because she saw the AI inference opportunity and AWS wasn't moving fast enough.

## Key Discussion Points

- **Problem**: Enterprise AI inference costs are exploding. Companies running real-time AI workloads (autonomous vehicles, manufacturing inspection, fraud detection) are spending millions on cloud GPU inference. Edge deployment reduces costs and latency but is technically complex and inflexible.

- **Solution**: CloudNest's routing engine dynamically splits model inference between edge nodes and cloud. Their algorithms determine in real-time which layers of a neural network should run at the edge vs cloud based on latency requirements, cost constraints, and accuracy thresholds. Result: 60% cost reduction on average.

- **Traction**: 18 enterprise customers. $2.4M ARR. Growing 30% QoQ. Key accounts include 3 Fortune 500 companies — notably a major automaker using CloudNest for autonomous driving inference.

- **Team**: 35 employees, primarily Berlin with 4 in SF. Natasha (CEO) from AWS edge. Kai Tanaka (CTO) was on NVIDIA's inference optimization team — wrote several of the key papers on TensorRT optimizations.

- **Fundraise**: Series A, targeting ~$18M. $6M seed from Atomico (2023).

## Portfolio Synergy

This jumped out at me: both CodeWeave and Spectra run significant inference workloads. CloudNest could directly reduce their infrastructure costs. This is the kind of platform investment that creates value across our portfolio.

## My Assessment

Natasha is the real deal. Deep technical credibility, clear market insight, and a strong team. The AI inference cost problem is only getting bigger as more companies move models to production. I want to move quickly on this.

- [ ] Sarah to check portfolio companies' inference spend to validate the value prop
- [ ] Request customer reference contacts from Natasha

title: CloudNest — Technical Deep-Dive with Kai Tanaka (CTO)
author: Maya Patel
content:
Meeting: Technical deep-dive — CloudNest
Date: March 15, 2026
Attendees: Maya Patel (AIVC), Kai Tanaka (CTO, CloudNest)
Location: Zoom + screen share (demo environment)

## Summary

2-hour session with Kai walking through the inference routing engine, model-splitting algorithms, and SDK integration. This is genuinely novel technology.

## Technical Architecture

- **Inference Routing Engine**: The core innovation. CloudNest dynamically determines, for each inference request, how to partition model execution across available infrastructure. The routing decision factors in: current latency at each node, cost per inference unit, accuracy requirements for the specific request, and current network conditions.

- **Model Splitting**: This is where it gets interesting. Rather than running the full model at either edge or cloud, CloudNest can split a neural network at specific layer boundaries and execute different segments on different hardware. Early layers (feature extraction) often run at edge; later layers (classification/generation) run in cloud. The split point is dynamically adjusted per request.

- **Benchmark Results**: Kai showed me benchmarks on standard ML models (ResNet-50, BERT, YOLOv5). Consistent 45-65% cost reduction across model types. Latency improvements of 20-40ms for real-time workloads. I validated these against published benchmarks for cloud-only inference — the numbers check out.

- **SDK Integration**: Clean design. Python SDK drops into existing ML serving frameworks (TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, Triton). 3 lines of code to wrap an existing inference call with CloudNest routing. Kai demoed it live — took about 5 minutes to integrate into a sample application.

## Competitive Moat Assessment

- **Strengths**: The dynamic model-splitting is genuinely hard to build. It requires deep understanding of neural network architecture, hardware-specific optimizations (different edge devices have different capabilities), and real-time optimization under uncertainty. Kai's NVIDIA background is directly relevant — he knows GPU execution at the hardware level.

- **Concern**: Cloudflare (Workers AI) and Fastly are building edge AI inference products. They have massive existing edge networks. If they add smart routing, could they replicate CloudNest's value prop? Kai's counter: their approach is "run the whole model at the edge" — they don't do model splitting, which is where the real optimization happens. He estimates CloudNest is 18 months ahead on the ML-specific optimizations.

## Technical Assessment

- **Innovation**: 8/10 — The dynamic model-splitting with real-time routing is novel and technically impressive. I haven't seen another company doing this at this level of sophistication.

- **Engineering Quality**: 8/10 — Clean architecture, well-designed SDK, strong benchmarks. Kai's team clearly knows what they're doing.

- **Defensibility**: 7/10 — The technology is hard to replicate but not impossible. Infrastructure giants (Cloudflare, AWS) could invest heavily. The 18-month head start is real but needs to be maintained.

## Action Items

- [ ] Maya to write up technical assessment for Sarah
- [ ] Request access to CloudNest's technical documentation for deeper review
- [ ] Explore whether CodeWeave or Spectra would be willing to do a trial

title: CloudNest — Commercial Deep-Dive with Natasha Volkov
author: Sarah Chen
content:
Meeting: Commercial deep-dive — CloudNest
Date: April 22, 2026
Attendees: Sarah Chen (AIVC), Natasha Volkov (CEO), Kai Tanaka (CTO)
Location: Zoom

## Summary

Deep commercial discussion covering revenue, go-to-market, and expansion strategy. Strong numbers with one significant challenge.

## Commercial Metrics

- **Revenue**: $2.4M ARR as of March 2026. Growing 30% QoQ. Was $1.4M at end of Q3 2025.

- **Customer Base**: 18 enterprise customers. Mix of Fortune 500 (3), mid-market tech companies (8), and growth-stage startups (7).

- **Expansion Revenue**: Net dollar retention is 135%. Customers land with one ML workload and expand to others. The automaker started with one autonomous driving model, now runs 12 models through CloudNest. This land-and-expand motion is organic — customers see the cost savings on one workload and migrate others.

- **Key Accounts**: The automaker's autonomous driving team is their largest account ($340K/year). Also serving a major financial services firm for real-time fraud detection, and a manufacturing company for quality inspection.

- **Unit Economics**: Average starting ACV $85K. Expands to $130K+ within 12 months. Gross margins 82%. CAC payback ~14 months.

## Go-to-Market Challenge

- Selling from Berlin to US enterprise is hard. Natasha acknowledged this directly. The 4-person SF team is primarily engineering. She's planning to hire a US-based VP of Sales and 3 AEs with Series A capital. This is the right move but it's a risk — the GTM motion is unproven at scale in the US.

- European traction is strong (10 of 18 customers) but the US market is where the biggest AI infrastructure budgets are.

## Competitive Dynamics

- Atomico led the seed and has pro-rata rights. They're likely to follow on but not lead. Natasha wants a US-based lead investor who can help with US GTM. This is an area where AIVC can add real value.

- Other investors showing interest: Coatue, IVP. Natasha is being selective — wants a lead who understands infrastructure.

## My Assessment

I like this deal a lot. The technology is strong (Maya confirmed), the traction is real, and the market timing is perfect — every company is struggling with AI inference costs. The US GTM buildout is the main risk, but that's exactly where we can help. I want to bring this to IC.

- [ ] Sarah to model out scenarios for US GTM ramp
- [ ] Check Atomico pro-rata terms and potential competitive dynamics
- [ ] Sarah to discuss IC timeline with David — need to move fast

title: CloudNest — Customer Reference Call (Automaker ML Platform Lead)
author: Maya Patel
content:
Meeting: Customer reference call — CloudNest
Date: May 20, 2026
Attendees: Maya Patel (AIVC), Thomas Weber (ML Platform Lead, [Major European Automaker])
Location: Zoom

## Summary

Strong customer reference. Thomas was enthusiastic and specific about CloudNest's impact.

## Key Points

- **Use Case**: Thomas's team runs real-time object detection models for the company's autonomous driving program. They process sensor data from test vehicles — cameras, lidar, radar — through neural networks that need sub-50ms latency for safety-critical decisions.

- **Before CloudNest**: All inference ran on cloud GPU instances (NVIDIA A100s on AWS). Monthly bill was approximately $600K. Latency was variable — 40-120ms depending on cloud load, which was unacceptable for real-time applications.

- **After CloudNest**: Inference now splits dynamically between edge compute units in the vehicles and cloud. CloudNest routes latency-critical inference to edge, batch processing and model updates to cloud. Monthly bill dropped to ~$270K (55% reduction). Latency stabilized at 15-35ms.

- **Quote**: "CloudNest cut our inference bill by 55% and reduced latency by 30ms on average. For our autonomous driving program, the latency improvement is actually more valuable than the cost savings — it directly impacts safety response times."

- **Expansion**: Started with one model (object detection), now running 12 models through CloudNest including path planning, sensor fusion, and predictive maintenance. Thomas said he would recommend CloudNest to peers.

- **Support Experience**: "Kai and his team are incredibly responsive. When we had an edge deployment issue during a vehicle test, they had a fix within 2 hours. That kind of support is rare."

- **Concerns**: Thomas mentioned that CloudNest's US support hours can be challenging given the Berlin-based team (time zone gap for urgent issues). He said the SF team addition has helped but it's not yet 24/7.

## Assessment

This is a strong reference. The use case is exactly the high-value, latency-critical scenario where CloudNest's technology shines. The willingness to recommend to peers is a good indicator of genuine satisfaction.

title: Edge AI Inference Market Heats Up as CloudNest Promises 60% Cost Reduction
author: James Anderson
content:
Edge AI Inference Market Heats Up as CloudNest Promises 60% Cost Reduction
By James Anderson | The Register | March 12, 2026

As enterprises rush to deploy AI models in production, a Berlin-based startup is betting that the future of inference isn't in the cloud or at the edge — it's in both.

CloudNest, founded in 2023 by former AWS edge computing lead Natasha Volkov and ex-NVIDIA inference engineer Kai Tanaka, has built a platform that dynamically routes AI inference between edge devices and cloud infrastructure. The company claims its technology can reduce inference costs by up to 60% while also improving latency for real-time applications.

The secret sauce, according to CTO Tanaka, is a technique called dynamic model splitting. "Most approaches to edge inference are all-or-nothing — you either run the entire model at the edge or in the cloud," Tanaka explained to The Register. "We split the model at the layer level, running compute-light feature extraction at the edge and compute-heavy classification in the cloud. The split point adjusts in real-time based on current conditions."

The company says it has 18 enterprise customers including a Fortune 500 automaker using the platform for autonomous driving inference. CloudNest, which raised a $6 million seed round from Atomico in 2023, is understood to be raising a Series A.

The edge AI inference market is increasingly crowded. Cloudflare launched Workers AI last month, bringing serverless AI inference to its global edge network. Fastly is building similar capabilities. And the cloud hyperscalers — AWS, Google Cloud, Azure — are all investing heavily in inference optimization.

But Volkov argues that infrastructure companies are approaching the problem from the wrong direction. "Cloudflare and Fastly are edge companies adding AI. We're an AI company that understands edge. That difference matters when you're optimizing neural network execution at the hardware level."

Analyst firm Gartner estimates the AI inference market will reach $45 billion by 2028, with edge inference growing at nearly twice the rate of cloud inference as latency-sensitive applications like autonomous vehicles, robotics, and real-time analytics demand faster response times.

title: Cloudflare Announces Workers AI: Serverless AI Inference at the Edge
author: Frederic Lardinois
content:
Cloudflare Announces Workers AI: Serverless AI Inference at the Edge
By Frederic Lardinois | TechCrunch | February 15, 2026

Cloudflare today announced the general availability of Workers AI, its serverless platform for running AI inference workloads on Cloudflare's global edge network spanning 300+ cities worldwide.

Workers AI allows developers to run popular machine learning models — including large language models, image recognition, and text classification — on Cloudflare's edge infrastructure without managing GPU instances. The platform supports models from Hugging Face, Meta (Llama), and others, with Cloudflare handling model deployment, scaling, and optimization.

"We believe AI inference will follow the same path as web content — moving from centralized data centers to the edge," said Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince. "Workers AI makes it trivially easy to run AI at the edge. No GPU provisioning, no infrastructure management, just write your code and deploy."

Pricing is per-inference-unit, with Cloudflare promising costs 50-70% below comparable cloud GPU instances for supported models. The platform currently supports over 40 pre-optimized models, with custom model deployment in beta.

The announcement positions Cloudflare directly against cloud GPU providers like AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, as well as startups like CloudNest and Modal that are building AI inference optimization platforms. Industry analysts noted that Cloudflare's massive existing edge network gives it a significant infrastructure advantage.

"Cloudflare is the most credible challenger to cloud-native AI inference," said Forrester analyst Michael Chen. "Their edge network is already deployed at scale. The question is whether their AI optimization is sophisticated enough for demanding workloads like autonomous driving or real-time video analysis."

The announcement sent ripples through the AI infrastructure startup ecosystem, with investors questioning whether venture-backed companies can compete with infrastructure giants adding AI capabilities.

title: Modal Raises $70M Series B for Cloud ML Infrastructure
author: Kyle Wiggers
content:
Modal Raises $70M Series B for Cloud ML Infrastructure
By Kyle Wiggers | VentureBeat | April 8, 2026

Modal, the cloud infrastructure company that lets developers run machine learning workloads without managing servers, has raised $70 million in Series B funding led by Redpoint Ventures with participation from a16z and existing investor Variant.

The San Francisco-based company, which has been growing rapidly since its public launch in early 2025, provides a serverless platform for compute-intensive workloads including ML model training, inference, and data processing. Modal abstracts away the complexity of GPU provisioning, container orchestration, and scaling, allowing ML engineers to focus on their models rather than infrastructure.

"We're building the cloud that AI developers actually want," said Modal CEO Erik Bernhardsson, who previously built the ML platform at Spotify. "The existing cloud providers were designed for web applications. ML workloads are fundamentally different — they're bursty, GPU-hungry, and data-intensive."

Modal says its platform now serves over 2,000 companies, up from 500 a year ago, with annual recurring revenue exceeding $25 million. Notable customers include AI startups, financial services firms, and gaming companies.

The fundraise comes as the AI infrastructure market continues to attract significant venture capital. CloudNest recently raised questions about edge-vs-cloud inference optimization, while CoreWeave raised $2.3 billion for its GPU cloud platform. The market is sorting itself into layers: GPU cloud providers (CoreWeave, Lambda), ML platforms (Modal, Anyscale), and optimization layers (CloudNest).

Modal's cloud-native approach contrasts with companies like CloudNest that focus on edge-cloud hybrid inference. Bernhardsson argues that for most workloads, cloud-native is still the right approach. "Edge inference is important for specific use cases like autonomous vehicles, but 90% of AI workloads run in the cloud and will continue to do so."
